#note: See @bib{RN117@206–207}: “In his transliteration of the opening lines of the tablet in Essays Pope (@bib{RN163@31}, Foster reads the end of the line as @i{úr-ba-ri} but without translating. There seem to be too many wedges present to read @akk{{giš}EREN} (so @bib{RN580@80, fn. 1}) and I have kept to the original reading of Jastrow and Clay. Tournay and Shaffer read @akk{[im-ta]-aq-qu₂-ut} (@bib{RN580@80, fn. 2}). The trace at the beginning of the line precludes this, but @akk{i#-[m]a-aq-qu₂-ut} is possible. As I understand it, Enkidu is describing his intense physical reaction to whatever terrifying and impossible undertaking (see l. 17) Gilgameš has proposed in the lacuna.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@208}: “The derivation of @i{uš-ta-li-pa} is unclear. @i{CAD} identifies the form as a III/1 perf. of @i{elēpum}, ‘to be tangled, crossed’, but comments that the meaning is uncertain. One might have expected @i{uštēlipā}. @i{AHw} enters it under a verb @i{alāpum} Št, ‘machten unbeweglich (??)’. I have translated ad hoc in the spirit of @i{CAD} and @i{AHw}. A less likely possibility is to read @i{uštallipā} < @i{šalāpum} II/1 perf., ‘to unsheath, pull out'. In the following line Enkidu complains of limpness of limbs and general weakness and it is not out of the question that this enfeeblement has affected his neck: ’sobs, my friend, have extracted the sinews from my neck’, i.e. he cannot hold his head up any more.” See also @bib{RN602@407}: “@i{uštālipā} ist ein reziproker Št₂-Stamm von @i{elēpu}: s. Rez., @i{ZA} 84 (1994) 164 f. Nr. 1.8 mit Ergänzung in @i{Verbalstämme} 121 Nr. 369. Übersetzung: ‘Klagen, mein Freund, haben meine Nackensehnen verspannt/verknotet.’”

#note: See @bib{RN117@210}: “Others have read at the beginning [@i{ša} @akk{{giš}}@i{er}]@i{ēnim}(eren) or even [@i{ša qišti er}]@i{ēnim} (for which room looks short, however written) but to my eyes the traces fit @i{ib-ri} better. What is restored before @i{ibrī} depends on how one construes what comes after. The reading adopted here goes back to Schott (@i{Reclam}²: “ich will ihren Berg ersteigen”). Though the verb @i{elûm} is very seldom construed with the object climbed in the accusative outside the fixed idiomatic usage of the same phrase, e.g. @i{šadâšu īli}, meaning a person disappeared-note the construction @i{ēlû šamāʾī} in l. 140 below and the repeated phrase @i{nīlû šadâ} in the late text (SB VIII 52, X 31 // 128 // 228). But there are other possibilities: (a) emend to @akk{lu-li a-<na> ša-di-ša}, (b) interpret the signs as @i{lūli aš-šadîša} (so @bib{ebeling1932review@228}; @bib{LS304@213}; @i{AHw}, p. 206; @i{CAD} E, p. 118), which would be an example, unique in this text, of the apocopated preposition prefixed to the noun, or (c) abandon the possessive suffix and boldly posit a new adverb, @i{šadîšam}, ‘mountainwards’ (cf. GAG §67g). Scott’s reading and solutions (a) and (b), with their fem. possessive, preclude the restoration of masc. @i{erēnum} and favour [@i{ša qištim}]. Solution (c) would make an anticipatory genitive of this sort unlikely and the old staple [@i{al-kam}] would then recommend itself.”

%n ṣiprū | šalāšā (||) manâ | ša ahīšina
#note: See @bib{RN117@212}: “A @i{ṣiprum} is typically a tapering projection like a horn or a comet’s tail (see @i{CAD} Ṣ, s.v.). Here the word occurs in a line that falls between those describing the daggers’ blades and pommels and are qualified as being ‘of the blades’ sides’. The reference can only be to a projecting crossguard that keep the user’s hand from slipping on to the blade (so already Labat: ‘crête de leur garde’). Good examples of blades furnished with such projections are the famous gold daggers from the royal cemetery at Ur. The curved guard projects out from the blade on either side in the manner of two horns or crests (photographs: Woolley, @i{UE} II, pls. 155, 157).”

In a dagger @i{iḫzu}s are most easily imagined as forming the main component of the hilt’s pommel, since soft metal and decoration are most appropriate to this part of a weapon.”

%n [...] ... | tuttēr | ana libbi (|) āli
#note: See @bib{RN117@214}: “Von Soden took the verb as II/2 preterite, restored @akk{[ina m]a-ti}, and translated ‘Wann würdest du zurückgebracht in die Stadt?’, but with the comment ‘es ist nicht klar, … was damit gemeint wird’ (@bib{LS304@214}; see similarly Reclam⁴⁻⁵ but note Reclam²: ‘bring zurück zur Stadt!’). Others have translated similarly (Dalley, Hecker), or as if the verb was a simple I/1 present, either as a question (Heidel, Labat, Bottéro, and, restoring @akk{[im-m]a-ti}, @bib{RN580@95, fn. 98}), a wish (Speiser) or a prediction (Pettinato). The verb is unsuited to a question relating to Gilgameš’s anticipated return--unless it is future perfect, i.e. II/1 transitive and notably lacks the ventive ending that would be expected if it referred to the hero’s homecoming. Apart from the problems raised by @i{tuttēr}, the first word is also open to doubt: Clay’s copy did not suggest that the broken sign could be @i{ma} and to my eyes it is more like @i{ne}. Rather than an interrogative, the broken word might be the object of transitive @i{tuttēr}.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@215}: “266–7. The ‘river of Ḫuwawa’ is otherwise unknown and does not quite ring true as the object of Gilgameš’s strivings: his stated ambitions are to defeat Ḫuwawa by force of arms and to fell the cedars under his protection. One thus has some sympathy for those who prefer @i{nârum}, ‘to slay’, to @i{nārum}, ‘river’, but Speiser’s rendering, ‘after the slaying of Ḫuwawa’, mistranslates @i{ina nârim}, which as an infinitive construction would mean ‘while slaying, by slaying'. As the text stands this would be a curious way of inciting Gilgameš to stand awash in Ḫuwawa’s blood and accordingly I have stayed with ‘river'.
